procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment of the Jammu & Kashmir High Court holding that the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, was validly extended to the State of Jammu and Kashmir by the Jammu and Kashmir (Extension of Laws) Act, 1956.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court decided the question of the validity of the extension of the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, on a reference made by the Special Magistrate under s. 432 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appeal to the Supreme Court was by special leave and was directed against the judgment of the Jammu & Kashmir High Court. The only question involved in the appeal before the Supreme Court was the validity of the extension of the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946.

decision.appeal_result: In the result the appeal fails and is dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, was validly extended to the State of Jammu and Kashmir by the Jammu and Kashmir (Extension of Laws) Act, 1956.

facts: The Jammu and Kashmir (Extension of Laws) Act, 1956 (Extension Act) received presidential assent on September 25, 1956. This Act provided for the extension of the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946 (DSPE Act) to the State of Jammu and Kashmir.
A government notification appointed November 1, 1956, as the date the Extension Act would come into force.
On the same day, November 1, 1956, the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, also came into force, which changed Delhi's status from a 'Part C State' to a 'Union Territory'.
law: The appellant argued that Parliament's power to extend the jurisdiction of a police force to another state is derived from Entry 80 of the Union List, which allows for the extension of powers of a police force 'belonging to any State'.

The appellant contended that since the DSPE Act was extended on November 1, 1956—the very day Delhi ceased to be a 'State'—Parliament no longer had the constitutional authority to extend the jurisdiction of the Delhi police force.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument by focusing on the date the law was passed, not the date it came into effect.
The Court reasoned that when Parliament passed the Extension Act on September 25, 1956, Delhi was still a 'Part C State'.
Therefore, at the time of enacting the law, Parliament was constitutionally competent to authorize the extension of the Delhi police force's jurisdiction.

The Court held that the power was validly exercised when the law was passed. The fact that Parliament may have lost this specific power on November 1, 1956 (when Delhi's status changed) did not retroactively invalidate the law that had already been competently enacted.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, was validly extended to the State of Jammu and Kashmir because Parliament had the constitutional competence to pass the Extension Act on the date it was enacted (September 25, 1956), when Delhi was still considered a State.

issue.issue_text: Whether the extension of the Act is invalidated by the fact that Parliament ceased to have the power to extend the jurisdiction of the Delhi Special Police Force after November 1, 1956, when Delhi ceased to be a Part 'C' State.

facts: The Jammu and Kashmir (Extension of Laws) Act, 1956, which extended the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act to Jammu and Kashmir, was passed and received presidential assent on September 25, 1956.
At the time the Extension Act was passed, Delhi was a Part 'C' State.
A government notification appointed November 1, 1956, as the date the extension would come into force.
On that same day, November 1, 1956, the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act came into force, and Delhi ceased to be a Part 'C' State and became a Union Territory.
law: The validity of a law is determined by the legislative body's competence at the time the law is enacted, not necessarily at the time it comes into force.
application: The Supreme Court focused on the moment the Extension Act was passed by Parliament, which was September 25, 1956.
On that date, Delhi was a Part 'C' State, and therefore Parliament had the constitutional power to extend the jurisdiction of its police force to another area.
The Court reasoned that since the power was validly exercised when the law was made, a subsequent change in Delhi's constitutional status did not invalidate the law itself.
The fact that Parliament may have lost the power to pass such a law *after* November 1, 1956, was deemed irrelevant to the validity of the law that was passed *before* that date.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the extension of the Act was valid because Parliament had the necessary constitutional power when it passed the Extension Act on September 25, 1956. The subsequent change in Delhi's status on the day the Act came into force did not retroactively invalidate the properly enacted law.

issue.issue_text: Whether Article 254 of the Constitution, concerning inconsistency between Union and State laws, applies to the present case.

facts: The case involves the extension of the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946 to the State of Jammu and Kashmir.
An argument was made that this Act was repugnant to and inconsistent with existing laws in Jammu and Kashmir, such as the J&K Code of Criminal Procedure and the J&K Police Act.
law: Article 254 of the Constitution deals with inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and laws made by State Legislatures, particularly concerning the Concurrent List.
Entry 80 of the Union List (List I) grants Parliament the power to legislate on the extension of powers and jurisdiction of a police force from one state to another area.
Article 246 gives Parliament exclusive power to make laws with respect to matters enumerated in the Union List (List I).
application: The Court found that the impugned law, the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, was fully covered by Entry 80 of the Union List.
At the time the Act was extended, Parliament did not have the power to make laws for Jammu and Kashmir with respect to items in the Concurrent List.

Since the law was based on Parliament's exclusive power under the Union List (Entry 80) and not the Concurrent List, the Court reasoned that Article 254, which governs inconsistencies involving the Concurrent List, could not apply.
The Court further clarified that because the legislation falls under Entry 80, it would override any repugnant state laws by virtue of Parliament's exclusive power under Article 246.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, concluding that Article 254 has no application to the present case because the impugned Act is a law made under Entry 80 of the Union List, not the Concurrent List.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The executive power to enforce a validly enacted law, or to bring it into effect, does not cease to exist merely because the legislative body that enacted the law has subsequently lost its legislative competence over that subject matter.
obiter: The learned counsel did not press the point regarding art. 1-l of the Constitution.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The executive power to implement a validly enacted and extended law, such as issuing a notification to bring it into force, does not cease to exist merely because the legislature's power to create that specific law has subsequently been altered or extinguished. The validity of the executive action is derived from the law as it stood when enacted and extended, and the general principle that executive power corresponds to legislative power is subject to constitutional exceptions that allow for the continued execution of existing laws.
legal_tests_applied: The principle from State of Assam v. Ka Bchyien. Kurka}ang, which holds that although a legislature's power to create new laws may end, the executive power conferred under a pre-existing, valid regulation to bring laws into force continues so long as that regulation remains on the statute book.

The interpretation of Article 73 of the Constitution, which establishes that the general principle of executive power corresponding to legislative power is not absolute and is subject to other constitutional provisions and exceptions, such as those found in Articles 277 and 372 concerning the continuation of existing laws.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's contention that the law could not be extended after Delhi's status changed was rejected because the power to issue the notification was derived from the existing, validly passed law, and this executive power was not destroyed by the subsequent constitutional amendment affecting legislative power.

The argument that the extended law cannot operate without a corresponding legislative power failed because the general principle in Article 73 is subject to constitutional exceptions, and the executive power to execute a validly enacted law does not cease simply because the power to make that law has been transferred or has ceased.

The attempt to invoke Article 254 regarding repugnancy was unsuccessful because the court determined the impugned law is covered by entry 80 of the Union List, not the Concurrent List, rendering Article 254 inapplicable.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act did not destroy the efficacy of the power to extend the Act, a position the court affirmed by applying the principle that executive powers granted by a valid law can survive changes to the legislature's authority.

The respondent's argument that the executive power to execute a valid law can persist even after the corresponding legislative power ceases was accepted by the court, which noted that no authority was cited to support the contrary position.

The respondent correctly identified that the impugned law falls under entry 80 of the Union List, which meant that Article 254, concerning inconsistencies with laws on the Concurrent List, could not be applied to the case.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning upholds the principle of legal continuity, ensuring that the executive power to execute a validly enacted law does not cease to exist simply because the power to make that law has been transferred to another authority or has ceased, thereby preventing a legal vacuum where valid laws become unenforceable due to subsequent constitutional or legislative changes.
